Hi Patrícia, it is Karen. A quick note before this afternoon's retrospective. I read your incident report and it was clear, so thank you for that. This afternoon is a different meeting, though. It is not about what happened. It is about what we should have done. I want three things from you. First, the moment where the process failed, not the person who was on the keyboard. Second, one thing we could have done faster, with the number of minutes it would have saved. And third, one action item that closes the gap for good. Keep it blameless. If somebody starts naming people, bring the room back to the process. You were the one closest to the customer, so your view of the gap is the one I need. See you at four.

Patrícia, it is Mark. Karen asked me to send you a short note before the retrospective, because this is the meeting where English gets dangerous. Should have and could have are strong words. Point them at yourself or at the process, and the room stays open: we should have checked the threshold, the alert should have been sent sooner. Point them at a person, and the room closes: you should have checked it. Nobody speaks after that, and the real cause stays hidden. So use we, or use the passive: the warning should not have been overlooked. And when you say could have, always add the number. We could have rolled back in ten minutes is worth a hundred times more than we could have been faster. Good luck this afternoon.
